prerequisites: Possess the knowledge of the primary subjects of Industrial Engineering and the ability to apply the fundamental techniques.

learning_outcomes.text: master the basic knowledge needed to address and solve problems encountered in professional chemical engineering practice
be able to identify, describe, and model basic transfer phenomena between phases and the main separation operations in the chemical industry
independently assess, based on the supported classroom activities, the relative importance of the transport phenomena involved in order to effectively simplify solution models
improve their professional communication skills through group work recommended by the instructors
adequately master further study, both institutional and independent, thanks to the discussions and cultural input provided in the classroom
identify and govern the phenomena that occur during separations
obtain useful information for the actual design of the equipment that he will meet later of studies
identify the nature, typology, time of contact, and transfer rate between the phases
know the physical phenomena that govern the unit operations
identify the most appropriate unit operation for a given separation problem
identify the operating parameters that influence separation performance
formulate and resolve mass balances both in analytical and graphic form
calculate the number of ideal stages necessary for a given separation
predict the effect of varying the operating parameters of separation equipment
know and apply the fundamental laws at the base of mechanical separations

syllabus_topics: Introductory framework of the subjects
Concept of unit operation
Description of the transfer phenomena between the phases in the primary unit operations
Driving force, thermodynamic limits and rate of transfer phenomena between phases
Principles of conservation and conservative entities: momentum, energy, matter
Transfer rate
Generalities on microscopic and macroscopic balances
Constitutive equations
Fundamental laws of the transfer: Newton, Fourier, Fick
Simple one-dimensional examples of transfer rate calculation
Fundamentals of fluid dynamics: laminar and turbulent motion, concept of head loss and coefficient of friction
Tools and methods for calculating the pressure drop in simple equipment
Bases of energy transport: conduction in solids, forced and natural convection in fluids
Tools and methods for calculating temperature profiles in simplified models
Transfer coefficients between phases and practical use of correlations and diagrams for their calculation
Fundamentals of matter transfer: binary diffusion in solids and fluids
Concept of analogy with energy transport with simple applications
Dimensionless groups and semi-empirical correlations
Main flow patterns
Reading and use of phase distribution diagrams for the main equilibrium cases, their construction starting from experimental data
Lever-arm rule, graphic techniques for calculating currents
Equilibrium stage concept with single stage calculation examples
Continuous and discontinuous equipments
General information on the flow diagrams in equi- and countercurrent
Physical and mathematical models of transfer equipment
Contact time
Double film model
Material balances around separation equipment
Graphic techniques for the resolution of balance equations, operating lines
Efficiency of the effective stage
Calculation of the equivalent number of theoretical stages
Concept of HTU and NTU
Examples of mechanical separations: filtration, ultrafiltration, centrifugation, cyclone separator

Case studies for practical application to the various unit operations on simple mixtures: absorption; flash vaporization; batch distillation; fractional distillation; liquid-liquid extraction, adsorption, leaching; mechanical separations.

assessment_methods.method: Oral exam (discussion of written paper and practical cases)

assessment_rules: The final assessment takes into account the student's overall performance based on a written and oral exam. The written test consists of three exercises, at least two of which must be addressed. The oral exam focuses on the discussion of the written paper and on practical cases. Sufficiency requires demonstrating the ability to identify methodological tools, correctly set up model equations, and indicate viable solutions. Excellence is achieved when the student can effectively deal with aspects not explicitly covered in class.
